claims.text: The starting material is as-received, mill-processed Q235 steel in its pre-exposure condition.
The interplay between an emergent oxide film and localized chloride attack governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in Q235 steel.
Increasing temperature accelerates passive-film breakdown and local dissolution at defects and grain boundaries in Q235 steel.
Aqueous 1 mol/L or 3.5 wt.% NaCl can be used as the corrosion medium.
The proposed comparison uses approximately 25 °C, 80 °C, and 150 °C exposure conditions.
The NaCl exposures are conducted under deoxygenated conditions.
EIS and potentiodynamic polarization are used to assess corrosion behavior in NaCl solution.
Oxide-film thickness, adhesion, and chemical composition mediate the corrosion response.
Inclusions and grain boundaries act as preferential corrosion-initiation sites.
Chloride ions penetrate microstructural flaws and undermine the protective function of the oxide scale.
Higher temperature increases passive-film dissolution rates and local reaction kinetics, promoting localized corrosion.
Relative to the room-temperature reference, elevated temperature will increase corrosion current density, shorten passivation intervals, and intensify localized attack.
Elevated-temperature degradation will be observable as EIS spectral shifts and deeper pits in ex situ SEM/EDS characterization.
Untreated Q235 steel in room-temperature NaCl develops a relatively stable oxide or pseudopassive layer with comparatively low corrosion current.
The proposed temperature-dependent film-breakdown effect may not apply outside the tested temperature range or in chloride-free environments.
Impurities and dynamic fluid conditions may alter the balance between oxide formation and dissolution in industrial environments.
Failure of elevated temperature to increase corrosion rate or film breakdown, together with stable or improved electrochemical behavior and minimal pitting, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
